docs.title: Matrix Multiplication example
docs.text: This tutorial has two parts: the first part is code optimization where techniques to optimize the matrix multiplication code are discussed, and the second part discusses how those techniques are automated by using the swiftpack decorator.

docs.title: Code optimization
docs.text: The optimization story behind ../../benchmarks/matmul_numba_bench.py is a classic GEMM workflow: start with a slow reference kernel, then progressively improve locality, backend compilation, and parallelism until the execution pattern matches the hardware more closely.

docs.title: 0- naive baseline
docs.text:
The simplest implementation is the direct triple loop:

def matmul_python_0(A, B, C):
    n = A.shape[0]
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            C[i, j] = 0.0
            for k in range(n):
                C[i, j] += A[i, k] * B[k, j]

This version is easy to verify and matches the mathematical definition, but it is dominated by Python-level loop overhead and poor memory access patterns. Each iteration performs Python object dispatch and repeated scalar updates, so it is orders of magnitude slower than optimized numerical kernels.

This baseline is useful because it establishes the reference behavior: the result is correct, but the implementation is far from efficient.

docs.title: 1- numba optimized
docs.text:
The first major improvement is to move the inner computation into Numba JIT code:

@njit
def matmul_numba_1(A, B, C):
    n = A.shape[0]
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            C[i, j] = 0.0
            for k in range(n):
                C[i, j] += A[i, k] * B[k, j]

Numba compiles the loop nest to machine code, eliminating much of the Python overhead. The algorithm is still the same, but the kernel now runs efficiently on the CPU. This is the point at which we see a large jump in throughput without changing the mathematical structure.

docs.title: 2- loop exchange
docs.text:
The next optimization is loop reordering. The naive kernel uses i, j, k order; the benchmark also compares other permutations such as i, k, j and j, i, k.

@njit
def matmul_2_ikj(A, B, C):
    n = A.shape[0]
    C.fill(0.0)
    for i in range(n):
        for k in range(n):
            for j in range(n):
                C[i, j] += A[i, k] * B[k, j]

The benefit comes from locality and reuse. With the i, k, j order, the code keeps a row of A and updates multiple C[i, j] entries as k changes, while B[k, j] is streamed in a way that better matches cache usage. This reduces the penalty from poor memory locality and often improves the compiled kernel substantially.

As a general rule, loop order matters because the innermost loop determines the stride pattern of memory access. Reordering loops is often the simplest way to improve a cache-friendly GEMM kernel.

docs.title: 3- compiler flags
docs.text:
Once the loop nest is structurally good, the next step is to let the backend aggressively optimize it:

@njit(fastmath=True)
def matmul_opt_flags_3(A, B, C):
    n = A.shape[0]
    C.fill(0.0)
    for i in range(n):
        for k in range(n):
            for j in range(n):
                C[i, j] += A[i, k] * B[k, j]

fastmath=True enables mathematically aggressive optimizations such as reassociation and vectorization-friendly transformations. These can increase throughput for floating-point kernels, especially when the code is numerically well-behaved and the result tolerances are not overly strict.

This optimization does not change the algorithm; it changes how the compiler is allowed to transform the kernel. It is a pure backend optimization, not a rewrite of the matrix formula.

docs.title: 4- parallelism
docs.text:
A high-level parallelism improvement is to parallelize the outer loop with prange:

@njit(parallel=True, fastmath=True)
def matmul_parallel_i_4(A, B, C):
    n = A.shape[0]
    C.fill(0.0)
    for i in prange(n):
        for k in range(n):
            for j in range(n):
                C[i, j] += A[i, k] * B[k, j]

This is a safe and effective parallel strategy because different values of i write to disjoint rows of C. Each thread can compute one output row independently, so the work is naturally parallelized.

The benchmark also compares other parallel choices such as prange over j or k, but the i-parallel form is especially natural for row-wise matrix multiplication. Parallelization can give an additional large gain once the single-threaded implementation is already efficient.

docs.title: 5- loop tiling
docs.text:
The final major optimization is loop tiling or blocking. Instead of processing the entire matrix in one pass, we work on sub-blocks that fit better into cache:

@njit(parallel=True, fastmath=True)
def matmul_blocked_parallel_5(A, B, C):
    n = A.shape[0]
    bs = BLOCK_SIZE
    C.fill(0.0)

    num_i_blocks = (n + bs - 1) // bs

    for b in prange(num_i_blocks):
        i_block = b * bs
        i_end = min(i_block + bs, n)

        for k_block in range(0, n, bs):
            for j_block in range(0, n, bs):
                k_end = min(k_block + bs, n)
                j_end = min(j_block + bs, n)

                for i in range(i_block, i_end):
                    for k in range(k_block, k_end):
                        for j in range(j_block, j_end):
                            C[i, j] += A[i, k] * B[k, j]

The key idea is to split the computation into tiles of size BLOCK_SIZE, so each block of A, B, and C fits in cache instead of streaming huge sections of the matrices through memory. This reduces cache misses and keeps the arithmetic core fed with data more efficiently.

The benchmark also explores blocked variants that use np.dot on submatrices and temporary buffers. These are closer to a high-performance BLAS-style GEMM and can be even faster when the tile size is chosen well.

The overall progression is shown in and can be summarized as:

  1. correct but slow Python triple loop,
  2. JIT compilation to remove interpreter overhead,
  3. loop reordering to improve locality,
  4. backend compiler flags for vectorization and reassociation,
  5. parallel outer loops with prange, and
  6. cache-aware tiling to reduce memory traffic.

The table summary is (copied from benchmark output):

Baseline Implementation GFLOP/s Abs Speedup Rel Speedup Correct 0_python_naive 0.014 1.00x 1.00x PASS 1_numba_naive 2.466 2.79x 2.79x PASS 2_order_ijk 2.466 2.79x 1.00x PASS 2_order_ikj 20.538 23.21x 8.33x PASS 2_order_jik 2.376 2.69x 0.12x PASS 2_order_jki 0.590 0.67x 0.25x PASS 2_order_kij 19.316 21.83x 32.74x PASS 2_order_kji 0.597 0.67x 0.03x PASS 3_fastmath_ikj 20.538 23.21x 34.42x PASS 4_parallel_i 20.546 23.22x 1.00x PASS 4_parallel_k 19.024 21.50x 0.93x PASS 4_parallel_j 2.581 2.92x 0.14x PASS 5_blocked_parallel_i 6.945 7.85x 2.69x PASS 6_blocked_np_dot 28.775 32.52x 4.14x PASS 7_blocked_temp_copy 30.491 34.46x 1.06x PASS 8_two_level_blocked_temp_np_dot 31.485 35.59x 1.03x PASS 9_blocked_zero_alloc 32.819 37.09x 1.04x PASS 10_np_dot 67.542 76.34x 2.06x PASS

Note. numbers are obtained from Intel(R) Core(TM) Ultra 7 265 with 20 cores and 40 threads, 30MB cache with avx2.

This progression is the core optimization story behind matrix multiplication in Numba and is exactly the pattern that swiftpack tries to automate.

docs.title: Code Representation and Optimization with Numba
Code Representation
docs.text: Code representation bridges human-readable source code and executable target instructions. Compilers parse and lower source code through multiple levels of Intermediate Representation (IR) to analyze semantics and apply performance optimizations.

docs.title: Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)
docs.text:
An Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) is a hierarchical, tree-structured representation of source code produced during syntactic analysis. It strips away purely syntactic tokens (such as semicolons, explicit parentheses, and whitespace) while retaining structural semantics, operator precedence, and parent-child execution scopes.

  • Nodes: Represent structural constructs such as operators (+, *), statements (if, while), or expressions (BinaryOp).
  • Leaves: Represent terminal operands, such as variable names (Name) or literals (Constant).
  • Usage: Used by parsers, linters, semantic analyzers, static security checkers, and source-to-source compilers.

docs.title: List of Instructions
docs.text:
Lowering an AST into a linear List of Instructions flattens the tree structure into sequential abstract machine instructions. This flat Intermediate Representation (IR) often uses Three-Address Code (3AC) or register-based bytecode instructions where each operation has at most three operands.

  • Characteristics: Simple instruction semantics (e.g., LOAD, ADD, STORE, JUMP_IF_FALSE).
  • Usage: Simplifies register allocation, instruction selection, and target machine code emission. In Numba, Python AST is lowered into Numba IR instructions (such as jump, branch, call, and assignment operations) before being passed to LLVM.

docs.title: Control Flow Graph (CFG)
docs.text:
A Control Flow Graph (CFG) is a directed graph $(V, E)$ that explicitly models all possible execution paths through a program unit (such as a function or subroutine).

  • Nodes ($V$): Basic Blocks containing sequential instructions.
  • Edges ($E$): Control transfers via conditional branches, unconditional jumps, or function calls.

docs.title: Basic Blocks
docs.text:
Basic blocks are sequences of instructions with no branches except at the end. They are the building blocks of control flow graphs.

CFG is applied to basic blocks.

docs.title: Code Optimization Techniques
docs.text:
Depending on the scope of optimization, code optimization is either Local Optimization (operating within a single basic block) or Global Optimization (operating across basic blocks within a CFG or across function boundaries via Interprocedural Analysis).

                ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
                │      Code Optimization Scope           │
                └───────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                                    │
          ┌─────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┐
          ▼                                                   ▼

┌────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────┐ │ Local Optimization │ │ Global Optimization│ │ (Single Basic Block│ │ (Across CFG / │ │ Scope) │ │ Interprocedural) │ └────────────────────┘ └────────────────────┘

Below is the classification of optimization techniques across four fundamental domains:

docs.title: 1. Loop Optimization
docs.text:
Loops represent the highest execution-density areas in programs. Optimizing loop bounds, array index access, and iteration order yields significant performance gains.

  • Loop Invariant Code Motion (Hoisting): Moves computations whose values do not change across iterations outside the loop header.
  • Loop Unrolling: Replicates the loop body to decrease loop overhead (branch checks, induction increment) and expose instruction-level parallelism (ILP).
  • Loop Tiling (Blocking): Reorganizes loop access patterns to fit within CPU L1/L2 cache lines, minimizing cache misses.
  • Loop Exchange (Permutation): Reorders nested loops to improve data locality and vectorization opportunities.

docs.title: 2. Data Structure Optimization
docs.text:
Optimizes memory access patterns, layout, and allocation overheads.

  • Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) vs. Array-of-Structures (AoS): Reorganizes struct memory layouts to optimize spatial cache locality and improve vectorization.
  • Scalar Replacement of Aggregates (SRA): Replaces aggregate objects/tuples with independent scalar variables that can fit directly in CPU registers.
  • Sparsity Exploitation: Detects and optimizes operations on sparse data structures (e.g., sparse matrices) to avoid unnecessary computations and memory accesses.

docs.title: 3. Function Optimization
docs.text:
Reduces call-stack overhead and optimizes calling conventions.

  • Function Inlining: Replaces a function call site with the body of the target function, eliminating call/return stack frames and enabling downstream compiler optimizations.
  • Dead Argument Elimination: Removes unused parameters from function signatures to eliminate unnecessary argument passing in registers or stack frames.
  • Tail Call Optimization (TCO): Replaces recursive function call stack frames with jumps when the call is in the tail position, converting recursion to $O(1)$ stack space.

docs.title: 4. Logic & Expression Optimization
docs.text:
Simplifies arithmetic and logical execution paths.

  • Constant Folding & Propagation: Pre-calculates constant operations at compile time (e.g., 3 * 8 $\rightarrow$ 24) and propagates known constant values through expressions.
  • Dead Code Elimination (DCE): Identifies and removes unreachable blocks or instructions whose outputs are never read.
  • Strength Reduction: Replaces expensive operations with faster equivalent operations (e.g., replacing x * 8 with bitwise shift x << 3, or x ** 2 with x * x).
  • Common Subexpression Elimination (CSE): Detects redundant expressions and reuses previously computed values instead of recalculating them.

docs.title: Local Analysis and Local Value Numbering
docs.text: Local analysis reasons about one basic block (a straight-line run of statements with a single entry and exit) at a time. Nothing learned in a block is assumed to hold in another one, which keeps the analysis cheap and safe.

docs.title: Enabling it: the lvn directive
docs.text:
LocalValueNumbering (../../src/swiftpack/lvn.py) is an ordinary Transformation. It is scheduled with the lvn directive in scheduler.py:

(LocalValueNumbering, {"directive": "lvn"})

check_legality returns True only when directive == "lvn" and the tree is an ast.Module or ast.FunctionDef. Otherwise TransformationPipeline logs ILLEGAL and skips the pass. LocalAnalysis remains as an alias of the class.

AutoTileAndParallelizeScheduler runs it first, so later passes see simplified code.

docs.title: How the code works
docs.text:
LocalValueNumberingTransformer is an ast.NodeTransformer.

Scopes. A stack of tables is kept. Each table holds a copy_propagation_table (name -> Name/Constant) and an expression_value_table (expression signature -> temporary name). Entering a function, if/else branch, loop body, or with body pushes a fresh table, and leaving pops it, so facts never cross block boundaries.

Optimizations, applied per assignment:

  1. Copy/constant propagation: after a = b or a = 10, later loads of a are replaced (alias chains are followed).
  2. Constant folding: arithmetic, unary, and comparison operations on constants are evaluated at compile time.
  3. Algebraic simplification: x + 0, x * 1, x * 0, x / 1, x ** 1, x ** 0, and similar.
  4. Common subexpression elimination (value numbering): each non-trivial expression is keyed by ast.dump of its structure. The first occurrence is assigned to a __swiftpack_lvn_N temporary; later occurrences in the same block reuse it.
  5. Dead code elimination: assignments to names that are never loaded and whose right-hand side is pure (names, constants, unary/binary ops) are removed.

Example:

x = a * b            __swiftpack_lvn_0 = a * b
y = a * b     ->     x = __swiftpack_lvn_0
return x + y         return x + __swiftpack_lvn_0

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Signatures are structural, so a + b and b + a are different values.
  • Assignments do not invalidate cached expressions that read the reassigned variable; this is safe only for single-assignment code within a block.
  • Dead code elimination only considers loads within the same statement list.

docs.title: Loop exchange
docs.text: The directive loop_exchange is used to reorder nested loops. It takes a tuple of loop variable names, e.g., ("j", "k"), and reorders the loops to match that order.

docs.title: Directive syntax
docs.text:
The scheduler tuple for the scheduler is:

   (LoopExchange, {"target_loops": ("j", "k")})

where target_loops is a tuple of loop variable names to reorder. The scheduler user directive is:

   @swiftpack(scheduler=[(LoopExchange, {"target_loops": ("j", "k")})])

docs.title: Legality check:
docs.text: The loop exchange transformation is legal if the specified loop variables exist within the nested loop hierarchy and the transformation does not violate any data dependencies. The legality checker generates a Data Dependence Graph (DDG) from the AST and evaluates all dependence distance vectors. Swapping two loop levels is proven legal if and only if no dependence vector becomes lexicographically negative (i.e., the first non-zero element in the permuted distance vector remains non-negative) after the exchange.

docs.title: Transformation:
docs.text: The transformation reorders the nested loops according to the specified order of loop variables. It updates the AST to reflect the new loop order, ensuring that the loop bodies are correctly nested and that the loop variables are updated accordingly.

docs.title: Loop Tiling
docs.text: The directive loop_tiling is used to block or tile loops (combining strip-mining and loop permutation) to dramatically improve cache locality and spatial reuse. It takes a target loop variable name (e.g., "i") and an optional block size (e.g., block_size=32).

docs.title: Directive syntax
docs.text:
The scheduler tuple for the scheduler is: 

   (LoopTiling, {"target_loop": "i", "tile_size": 32})

where target_loop is the loop variable to tile and tile_size is the number of iterations per tile. The default tile size is 32. The scheduler user directive is: 

   @swiftpack(scheduler=[(LoopTiling, {"target_loop": "i", "tile_size": 32})])

docs.title: Legality check:
docs.text: The loop tiling transformation is legal if the target loop exists within the loop hierarchy and carries no backward (negative) distance dependencies. The legality checker generates a Data Dependence Graph (DG) and evaluates the distance vector components corresponding to the target loop level. Tiling is proven safe if all dependence vector entries for the targeted dimension are greater than or equal to zero ($\ge 0$), guaranteeing that block execution order does not violate program semantics or causality.

docs.title: Transformation:
docs.text: The transformation performs strip-mining on the target loop, splitting it into two nested loops: * Outer Tile Loop (_tile): Steps through the iteration space in increments equal to the specified block_size. * Inner Point Loop: Iterates locally within the current tile block, bounded by the tile boundaries. bounded by min(tile_start + block_size, upper_bound). The original loop body is safely nested inside the inner loop, preserving all variable bindings and computational logic.

docs.title: Loop Parallelism
docs.text: The directive LoopParallelism is used to enable multithreaded execution across iterations of a target loop (such as lowering to OpenMP or parallel runtimes via prange). It takes a loop variable name, e.g., "i".

docs.title: Directive syntax
docs.text:
The scheduler tuple for the scheduler is:

   (LoopParallelism, {"loop_var": "i"})

where loop_var is the loop variable to parallelize. The scheduler user directive is:

   @swiftpack(scheduler=[(LoopParallelism, {"loop_var": "i"})])

docs.title: Legality check:
docs.text: The loop parallelism transformation is legal if and only if the target loop carries no loop-carried dependencies. The legality checker analyzes the Data Dependence Graph (DDG) and inspects the distance vector components at the depth of the target loop variable. If all distance entries for that loop level are equal to 0 (indicating no cross-iteration hazards), the loop is proven safe for parallel execution. Any non-zero distance indicates a data race hazard, causing the legality check to fail.

docs.title: Transformation:
docs.text: The transformation searches the AST for the For loop matching the specified loop_var and replaces its iterator function from sequential range() to parallel prange(), enabling concurrent scheduling across available thread pools or hardware execution lanes.

docs.title: Loop unrolling
docs.text: The directive LoopUnrolling is used to replicate the body of a loop multiple times, reducing branch overhead and expanding Instruction-Level Parallelism (ILP). It takes a target loop variable name (e.g., "k") and an unrolling factor (e.g., factor=4).

docs.title: Directive syntax
docs.text:
The scheduler tuple for the scheduler is:

   (LoopUnrolling, {"loop_var": "k", "factor": 4})

where loop_var is the loop variable to unroll and factor is the number of times to replicate the loop body. The scheduler user directive is:

   @swiftpack(scheduler=[(LoopUnrolling, {"loop_var": "k", "factor": 4})])

docs.title: Legality check:
docs.text: Standard scalar loop unrolling is always legal for inner loops because duplicating independent scalar iteration bodies does not alter data dependence distances or execution ordering across iterations. The legality check verifies that the specified loop_var exists in the targeted loop scope.

docs.title: Transformation:
docs.text: The transformation modifies the loop AST in two ways: 1. Stride Scaling: Multiplies the step size of the loop's range() iterator by the specified factor (e.g., stepping by 4 instead of 1). 2. Body Duplication & Index Offsetting: Replicates the loop body factor times, substituting the loop variable with static index offsets (i, i + 1, i + 2, etc.) in subsequent unrolled copies.

docs.title: Transformation Pipeline
docs.text:
@swiftpack compiles a decorated function by retrieving its Python source, parsing it into an AST, and removing the @swiftpack decorator from the function definition. The configured scheduler creates an ordered transformation plan. For each step, the pipeline instantiates the transformation class and checks legality against the current AST. Illegal steps are logged and skipped; legal steps are applied in order and logged as successful.

After the passes run, the compiler ensures the result is an ast.Module, fixes missing source locations, compiles the AST, and executes it to retrieve the transformed function. The function is then wrapped with Numba's njit. The compiler makes prange available to the transformed function's globals.

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
A scheduler implements schedule(tree) and returns an ordered list of (TransformationClass, kwargs) pairs. The tree is the input function's AST; each kwargs dictionary is passed to that transformation's check_legality and, if legal, its apply method.

AutoTileAndParallelizeScheduler is the default. It schedules these passes in order:

  1. LocalValueNumbering with directive="lvn".
  2. LoopExchange with target_loops=("j", "k"), to reorder loops from IJK to IKJ for cache locality.
  3. LoopTiling with tile_size=32.
  4. ParallelizeLoop with loop_var="i", to parallelize the outermost i loop.

Use the scheduler argument to @swiftpack to provide a custom scheduler. The decorator uses parallel=True and fastmath=True for Numba by default; additional keyword arguments are passed to njit.

docs.title: Supported Transformations
docs.text: The default schedule includes LocalValueNumbering, LoopExchange, LoopTiling, and ParallelizeLoop. A transformation must implement check_legality(tree, **kwargs) and apply(tree, **kwargs). The pipeline only applies a pass when its legality check returns true.

docs.title: Adding a pass
docs.text:
1. Implement a Transformation subclass with check_legality and apply methods that accept the AST and any pass-specific keyword arguments.
  2. Import the class in scheduler.py and include (YourTransformation, {"option": value}) in the desired position in a scheduler's returned plan. The kwargs are passed to both methods.
  3. The apply method should return the updated AST. The pipeline feeds that result into the next legality check and transformation.
